name: Dexatrim
lead: Dexatrim is a brand of over-the-counter weight-loss products sold as appetite suppressants and energy aids. People use it to eat less and keep up energy during a calorie deficit, with the aim of losing body fat and looking leaner. The line was introduced in 1976 by Thompson Medical Company and originally relied on phenylpropanolamine (PPA), a sympathomimetic also used in cold remedies [1][3].

After regulatory action in 2000 PPA was removed, and current capsules are multi-ingredient stimulant blends built around caffeine, green tea extract, ginseng and other botanicals [2][3]. Ownership passed from Thompson Medical to Chattem in 1998 and the brand was sold to NVE Pharmaceuticals in 2014 [3].

PPA-era Dexatrim appears in the medical literature mainly through safety case reports, including a myocardial injury case in a young woman using the product at labelled amounts and a case of transient memory loss and aphasia [4][5]. Researchers also published a pharmacokinetic study of the controlled-release caplet [6]. No randomized trials of current Dexatrim formulations were found, and Wikipedia describes evidence for its individual ingredients as limited [3].

paras: Dexatrim is marketed to support appetite control, energy and calorie burning alongside a reduced-calorie diet [2]. Wikipedia lists current capsule products such as Max Complex 7, Max Daytime Appetite Control, Natural Green Tea and Natural Extra Energy [3]. Ingredient lists differ by product, and reported components include caffeine, green tea extract, Asian ginseng and DHEA [3]. Because the products are dietary supplements, the manufacturer states that the FDA has not evaluated its claims [3].

PPA is chiefly a norepinephrine-releasing agent, so it activates adrenergic receptors indirectly; Wikipedia describes it as a substituted amphetamine closely related to ephedrine and says its effects are mostly peripheral [8]. In a 1990 study of 12 volunteers, a 75 mg PPA controlled-release caplet taken once daily was compared with a 25 mg PPA solution taken three times daily for four days, measuring bioavailability and cardiovascular safety [6]. Current products rely on caffeine for stimulation, green tea extract for its catechins and ginseng for energy, according to Wikipedia and Grokipedia [3][2].

Dexatrim launched in 1976 under Thompson Medical, initially built around PPA [2]. One variant, Dexatrim-18, was advertised as suppressing appetite for 18 hours, and Grokipedia reports that this claim was challenged for lack of supporting pharmacokinetic evidence; Grokipedia is AI-generated and this detail is unverified [2]. In 2000 the FDA asked manufacturers to stop marketing PPA-containing drug products after a Yale study linked PPA to hemorrhagic stroke, and Dexatrim was reformulated [3]. The 2004 US ban on ephedra affected later versions that had used it [3].

Grokipedia reports that Dexatrim marketing in the late 1970s and 1980s used television and magazine campaigns with testimonials and slogans, and that in April 1983 Thompson Medical agreed to change some packaging claims; these details come from an AI-generated source and are presented as reported [2]. On PPA itself, Wikipedia says the FDA issued a public health advisory in November 2000 recommending against its use and asking companies to stop marketing it, estimated that it caused 200 to 500 strokes a year among users aged 18 to 49, and removed its over-the-counter status in 2005; Canada withdrew it in May 2001 [8].

A 2003 case report described myocardial injury in a young woman who used Dexatrim (PPA) at recommended doses for weight control, noting earlier links between PPA and hypertension and hemorrhagic stroke, particularly in younger women [4]. A 1984 case report described acute memory loss and nominal aphasia in a 36-year-old woman after using Dexatrim Extra Strength, resolving within 36 hours of stopping [5]. A survey of 100 people with eating-disorder symptoms found that 64% used an herbal product for weight loss, illustrating that such supplements are used in vulnerable groups [7].

For current formulations, Wikipedia lists caffeine-related effects such as insomnia, anxiety and palpitations, and notes possible liver concerns with green tea extract and androgenic effects with higher DHEA intake [3]. Labels advise against use in pregnancy or with heart conditions [2].

No randomized trials of Dexatrim for weight loss were found. Published human work consists of a 1990 pharmacokinetic and cardiovascular-safety study of a PPA controlled-release caplet in 12 volunteers [6] and individual case reports [4][5]. Wikipedia notes that no over-the-counter weight-loss supplement has met criteria for physician recommendation, and that evidence for several of its ingredients is insufficient [3].

Dexatrim was a household name among US diet pills in the 1980s and 1990s and remains in drugstores in its multi-ingredient form [3]. In T Nation threads it comes up as a casual reference for diet pills: one user said they cheated on a diet by taking Dexatrim 'to suppress the appetite a bit', another listed dexatrim alongside an ECA-type stack as an option for weigh-in preparation, and a trainer remarked on clients returning to 'dexatrim land' when frustrated with diets [9][10][11].

lore.intro: On T Nation, Dexatrim shows up in passing as a mainstream diet pill, mentioned by lifters who tried it as teenagers or used it to curb appetite during dieting or weight cuts.[9][10][12]

claims.claim: Dexatrim suppresses appetite enough to make cutting diets easier.
claims.believers: A poster on a dieting log said they took Dexatrim to suppress appetite and that it perhaps worked 'a little TOO well'.[9]
claims.experts: No randomized trial of current Dexatrim formulations has been published; Wikipedia says evidence for several ingredients is insufficient.[3]

claims.claim: Dexatrim is an alternative to ECA stacks for making weight before a fight.
claims.believers: One poster listed Dexatrim as an option next to an ECA-type stack for weigh-in preparation, noting it was banned in its older form.[10]
claims.experts: The FDA asked for PPA products to be withdrawn in 2000, after which Dexatrim was reformulated; case reports link PPA-era Dexatrim to cardiac and neurological events.[3][4][5]

claims.claim: Dexatrim from the PPA era carried stroke risk.
claims.believers: A forum poster listing drug side effects described Dexatrim as associated with fatal strokes.[13]
claims.experts: The FDA's 2000 advisory cited an increased risk of hemorrhagic stroke from PPA, estimated at 200 to 500 strokes a year in people aged 18 to 49.[3][8]

card.summary: A long-running diet-pill brand that dropped PPA after stroke concerns and now sells caffeine and green-tea blends with little trial evidence.
card.note: Original PPA formula was withdrawn after FDA action in 2000; case reports describe cardiac and neurological events.

quick.overview:
Dexatrim is an over-the-counter diet pill brand sold since the 1970s. It is marketed for appetite control and energy while dieting.

Its original ingredient, phenylpropanolamine, was removed after the FDA's 2000 action. Current versions use stimulant and botanical blends, and no trials of the branded products were found.
quick.mechanism: Earlier versions used a sympathomimetic amine that reduces appetite. Current versions rely on caffeine, green tea extract and other ingredients marketed to raise energy expenditure, though evidence for these ingredients is limited.
quick.risks: PPA-era use was linked in case reports and a Yale study to hemorrhagic stroke, heart injury and neurological effects. Current stimulant blends carry caffeine-type effects such as insomnia and palpitations, and labels advise caution with heart conditions and pregnancy.

chain: Stimulant ingredients reduce hunger and raise alertness
Lower body fat and a leaner look
angle.text: Dexatrim is taken to blunt appetite and add energy during a reduced-calorie diet, the idea being that eating less over weeks produces lower body fat and a leaner face and physique. The product's own marketing positions it as an aid alongside diet and exercise.
